dataset.name: Guarea guidonia and Ocotea sintenisii physiological and climate data for Tropical Responses to Altered Climate Experiment (TRACE) canopy tower site at Sabana Field Research Station, Luquillo, Puerto Rico in summer 2017
description: This data publication includes data collected as part of a study assessing physiological acclimation of canopy leaves at the Tropical Responses to Altered Climate Experiment (TRACE) canopy access tower, located at the Sabana Field Research Station in the Luquillo Experimental Forest, Puerto Rico. Physiological acclimation was assessed on two tree species, Guarea guidonia and Ocotea sintenisii, through photosynthetic and respiratory temperature response in the summer of 2017. Leaves were heated +3 ºCelsius throughout the canopy access tower using heating pads. Complementary environmental data were collected describing leaf temperature at each tower level where leaves were heated. Leaf area index was also measured at each level of the canopy access tower.

measurementTechnique:
STUDY DESIGN
The study was conducted at the Tropical Responses to Altered Climate Experiment (TRACE) site located at the Luquillo Experimental Forest. The experiment was conducted on a 20.1 m canopy tower (UpRight Inc., Dublin, Ireland). Access levels of the canopy tower were positioned every 1.8 meters (m), where each “Canopy Level” in the data sheets can be multiplied by 1.8 to get the height of the leaf in meters. The canopy tower was located in the same proximity but outside of the understory warming experiment. Individual leaves from two common canopy species, Ocotea sintenisii and Guarea guidonia, were heated +3 °C higher than the temperature of a nearby control leaf. Full expanded leaves were heated between 16-33 days, with a total of ~30 heated/control pairs. Heated leaf temperatures were controlled using a relay module (SSR-25 DA, Fotek Controls Co., Taiwan) that turned the heating pad (100 watt 120VAC, 24100k Kat’s Five Star Manufacturing Group Inc., Springfield, TN, USA) off when the leaf temperature read higher than 3 °C above the associated control leaf. Thermocouples were used to measure leaf temperature (TT-T-30 SLE(ROHS), OMEGA Engineering Inc., Norwalk, CT, USA). The thermocouples were wired into a multiplexor (AM25T, Campbell Scientific Inc., Logan, UT, USA) and temperature was recorded using a datalogger (CR1000, Campbell Scientific Inc.). Leaves were heated throughout the forest canopy from 1.8-19.8 m height.
Leaf gas exchange and chlorophyll fluorescence was measured after approximately one month of warming. The leaf heaters were turned off and photosynthesis was measured during the daytime. The following night, leaf respiration and chlorophyll fluorescence were measured on the heated and control leaves. Leaves were then collected and leaf traits (nitrogen per unit mass, nitrogen per unit area, leaf carbon to nitrogen ratio, leaf mass per area, percent leaf water content) were measured.
DATA COLLECTION - PLANT PHYSIOLOGY
Infrared gas analyzer: LI6400 (Li-Cor Inc., Lincoln, NE, United States) was used for all gas exchange measurements. The temperature of the chamber was adjusted outside of the normal instrumental range by cycling hot or cold water through the Expanded Temperature Control Kit (6400-88, Li-Cor Inc.) (see Carter et al. 2021 for more details). Net photosynthetic (Anet) temperature response curves were collected using the fluorescent head, collected measurements at 25, 27, 30, 33, 35, 37, and 40 °C leaf temperature. CO₂ concentration was controlled 400 parts per million (ppm) and light was controlled at saturating PPFD (photosynthetic photon flux density), at either 800 or 1200 micromoles per square meter per second (μmol m-2 s-1), and flow was controlled to keep vapor pressure deficit between 1 and 4 kilopascal (kPa). Respiratory temperature response curves were collected using a 6400-088 conifer chamber wrapped in aluminum foil. Curves were constructed by measuring CO₂ exchange of each leaf at 25, 30, 35, 37, and 40 °C. CO₂ concentrations were controlled at 400 ppm (see Carter et al. 2021 for more details).
DATA COLLECTION - ENVIRONMENTAL
Leaf temperature: Surface temperature of the leaves were measured beginning May 22, 2017 and ending August 18, 2017 using thermocouples attached to the adaxial side of the leaf. The actual start date of warming each leaf was staggered so that leaves were not measured and collected at one time period after their one month of warming.
The light environment at each canopy height was measured using two canopy analyzers (LAI-2000 and LAI-2200, Li-Cor Inc.) on July 6, 2017 and August 8, 2017.
For more information about the collection of these data see Carter et al. (2021).
